expression_help: Expressions are plain boolean sentences. Names are levers and fields on the node being checked (identifiability, scores, role), or results worked out so far (A4, outcome, highest_tier), or lists defined in this file (safety_categories). Operators: && (and), || (or), ! (not), == != >= <= > <, x in [list], not in. Functions: any(type), any(type, condition), count(type, condition), all(type, condition), overlaps(list, list), subset(list, list). Text goes in single quotes.

tier_rules.note: Checked top to bottom for each data node. The first one that matches sets the tier.

rules.because: it contains special category or safety-critical data
nobody can be picked out from it
it says something about how a named person is doing

pseudonymisation_credit.effect: Pseudonymised data keeps its content tier for the DPA question (the supplier still holds personal data), but counts one tier lower for screening severity. When no data in the flow is named, and there is no special category, safety or biometric data, the screening outcome and the AI use case floor each drop one step.
pseudonymisation_credit.why: Policy choice, not law. Turn it off by setting enabled to false.

0.label: Nothing personal
0.plain: Nobody could be picked out from it.
0.examples: Totals, anonymous survey results, lesson plans, generic templates.

1.label: Account basics
1.plain: It shows who someone is, but nothing about them.
1.examples: Names, work emails, job titles, logins, how often someone used something.
1.can: Outside tools are fine, as long as the company has signed a data protection agreement.

2.label: About a named person
2.rule: Sanctioned routes only. DPIA screening every time.
2.plain: It says something about how a named person is doing.
2.examples: Marks, attendance, feedback, essays, support notes, behaviour.
2.can: Only through the tools the organisation has approved, and always with a quick screening.

3.label: Special category
3.rule: Never leaves organisation systems. No AI.
3.plain: The most sensitive kind. A leak could really hurt someone.
3.examples: Health, SEND, safeguarding, ethnicity, religion, sexuality, anything about crime.
3.can: Keep it inside the organisation's own systems. No AI tools.

sanctioned.note: Per organisation. Keyed by company id or product id from products.json. max_tier is the highest tier that may flow to it. ai says whether its AI features are approved for personal data. A company not on this list may take Tier 1 at most.

policy.note: Plain words for the 'does your policy allow it?' answer. 'Policy' means this organisation's approved list below (sanctioned), never the supplier's. When the ceiling comes from a product's plan, the answer says it rests on the supplier's published terms and when they were checked. {company}, {tier}, {max_tier}, {plan}, {checked}, {version}, {owner}, {review_date} are filled in.
policy.source: Your organisation's approved list: rules table v{version}, owner {owner}, reviewed {review_date}.
policy.unowned: That list hasn't been given an owner or a review date yet, so treat these answers as a starting point, not your policy. The Rules page is where it's set.
policy.allowed: Your approved list says {company} may take up to Level {max_tier}. This sends Level {tier}, so that's fine.
policy.allowed_plan: {company}'s published terms for {plan} (checked {checked}; verify before relying on them) put it at Level {max_tier} under your rules. This sends Level {tier}, so that's fine.
policy.unlisted: {company} isn't on your approved list, so the default for anything unlisted (Level {max_tier}) applies. If your policy approves {company} for Level {tier}, add it to the list on the Rules page and this changes.
policy.allowed_inside: Nothing personal leaves the organisation, so no outside company needs approving.
policy.allowed_partner: {company} decides things with you, so it's a joint controller: you need a sharing agreement rather than a supplier contract. Level 3 data still never leaves.
policy.no_unlisted: No. {message} {company} isn't on your approved list, so the default applies. If your policy approves it for Level {tier}, add it to the list on the Rules page and this changes.

blocked.note: Checked for every wire carrying personal data. Names: tier, max_tier, company, to_role (the company's role on this flow), plan_note (" on the business plan" when the tool has plans), data, into_ai (the wire goes into an AI system), via_ai (either end is AI), ai_approved, crosses. A blocked wire turns red and produces no paperwork.

rules.message: Level 3 data never leaves organisation systems.
ways_out: Take the special category data out of {data}.
Keep it inside, on an organisation system.

rules.message: Level 3 data can't go into AI.
ways_out: Take the special category data out of {data}.
Do this step without AI.

rules.message: {company}{plan_note} is allowed up to Level {max_tier}; this wire carries Level {tier}.
ways_out: Send less: cut {data} down to what Level {max_tier} allows.
Use a sanctioned route, or a plan that's approved for Level {tier}.

rules.message: {company}'s AI features are not approved for personal data.
ways_out: Anonymise {data} first.
Use an approved AI route instead.

locks.reason: Learners, patients and people in care are always treated as vulnerable.
AI is always innovative technology for screening.

screening.text: Evaluating personal data to make automated, AI-assisted or similarly significant decisions about individuals
Using special category or criminal offence data
Systematic monitoring of individuals or a public place
screening.because: {title} runs continuously across a whole group

screening.text: Evaluation or scoring, including profiling or prediction
Matching or combining datasets from different purposes or sources
Personal data about children or other vulnerable individuals
A breach could jeopardise physical health or safety
AI, machine learning, generative AI or innovative technology
Collecting personal data without a privacy notice
New personal data from a third party
Existing data used for a new purpose
screening.because: {title} was held for a different reason

screening.text: Data of a highly personal nature

screening.because: {title} could block access or a right

plain.not_required: You don't need a full risk assessment. Keep the screening record with the flow.
plain.recommended: A short risk assessment is a good idea, but not a must. The DPO will say how far to take it.
plain.required: You need a full risk assessment (a DPIA) before this goes ahead. The canvas fills in most of it; a person does the rest.

use_case_floor.note: The AI node's use case sets a minimum. The outcome can be raised to meet it, never lowered.

levels.label: Approved use case and risk assessment
DPO approval, screening with the AI block
Full DPIA and assessment governance sign-off
High risk: DPO and executive sign-off, consider ICO consultation

bright_lines.note: Hard stops. A flow that hits one shows the reason and the ways out, and goes no further until it's fixed. Everything else is not a verdict: it goes to a named risk owner, who decides with the DPO's advice. Keep this list short; 'no' should be rare. 'kind' is stop (fix it first) or consult (the ICO must be consulted unless the risk comes down). Checked per node of 'type', or once for the whole flow when type is 'flow'.

rules.when: tier >= 1 && lawful_basis == 'consent' && any(people, group in power_imbalance_groups)
rules.title: Consent won't hold here
rules.say: {title} relies on consent, but students and staff can't freely say no to the organisation that teaches or employs them. The ICO says consent will not usually be valid where there's an imbalance of power.
ways_out: Use a different lawful basis, usually public task for a school or college.
If no other basis fits, this can't go ahead as designed.

rules.title: Under-13s can't give this consent
rules.say: {title} relies on consent, but a child under 13 can't consent to an online service themselves in UK law (DPA 2018 s.9); a parent or guardian has to.
ways_out: Use a different lawful basis, usually public task for a school.
If consent really is the only basis, get it from a parent and record how.

rules.title: No legal reason to use it
rules.say: Nobody could name a lawful basis for {title}. Without one, nothing else can make this lawful.
ways_out: Ask the DPO which basis could apply.
Leave {title} out.

rules.title: There's a less intrusive way
rules.say: You said {title} could be done with less data. If a gentler design gets the same result, the more intrusive one isn't justified.
ways_out: Build the less intrusive version instead. The 'make it easier' box may show it.
If the extra data really is needed, change your answer and say why.

rules.title: People's rights can't be honoured
rules.say: If someone can't see their data, have it deleted or have a decision explained, that's a flaw in the design, not a risk to weigh up.
ways_out: Pick a tool or design where data can be found, exported and deleted.
Make sure any automated result can be explained by a person.

rules.title: {title} won't sign up to our terms
rules.say: {title} won't agree to a data protection agreement that keeps them to our instructions. That's a contract fact, not a risk score.
ways_out: Use a supplier that will sign.
Send {title} nothing personal.

rules.title: {title} trains on your data
rules.say: {title} can use what you send to train its models, so people's data leaves your control for good.
ways_out: Get training switched off in the contract, then turn this off.
Send {title} nothing personal, or use an approved route.

rules.title: Data leaves the UK with no protection
rules.say: {title} holds data outside the UK and there's no transfer mechanism in place.
ways_out: Get an IDTA or UK addendum signed.
Choose UK or EU hosting.

rules.title: The ICO would need to be consulted
rules.say: As drawn, this combines warning signs the ICO treats as high risk: automatic decisions that can block vulnerable people, or biometrics of children. If that risk can't be brought down, the law says you must consult the ICO before starting.
ways_out: Put a person in charge of every decision.
Leave the biometrics out.
Then rerun the screening.

notes.say: This is already running, so the check is late. Do it now anyway: it's the only way to fix what it finds.

verdict.label: No, not like this
verdict.say: This hits a hard line. Each one below says why, and how to get past it.

verdict.label: Not this way
verdict.say: Your organisation's policy doesn't allow this route. The red wire says why, and gives two ways out.

verdict.label: Only after asking the ICO
verdict.say: Try the ways out first. If the risk stays high, the ICO must be consulted before this starts.

verdict.label: Yes, if someone senior signs it off
verdict.say: Some risk is left, and someone with the authority to change the project has to accept it in writing. Say who under 'Who decides'. The DPO advises; they don't approve.

verdict.label: Yes, once {risk_owner} signs it off
verdict.say: Once the to do items are done, {risk_owner} decides whether to accept the risk that's left, in writing. The DPO's advice is recorded either way.

verdict.label: Yes, once these are done
verdict.say: This can go ahead once the items marked to do are done.

verdict.label: Yes
verdict.say: Nothing left to do. Keep the screening record with the flow.

always_human.note: Printed on every document. The tool never declares a flow lawful. The sign-off lines follow the ICO template: measures, residual risk and DPO advice are signed separately.
always: A person signs the screening record. The canvas answers the questions; it does not approve anything.
when_full_dpia: Consultation with the people affected (DPIA step 3)
Scoring the likelihood and severity of each risk (DPIA step 5)
The risk owner approves the measures and accepts the risk that's left, in writing
DPO advice is recorded as accepted or overruled, with reasons if overruled

cheapest_change.note: For each candidate whose 'when' matches a node, the engine re-runs the rules with that one change. A change that clears a red wire or a hard line beats one that doesn't; then the one that removes the most open requirements wins; ties go to the first in this list, so the plan change (cheap, and doesn't change the idea) sits first.

candidates.cost: A paid business plan, roughly £20 a seat a month.
candidates.how: Move the people who use it onto the organisation's business plan, so a contract and no-training terms apply, and stop using personal logins.

candidates.cost: Outputs can't use the person's name; someone matches them back afterwards.
candidates.how: Swap names for a code (a candidate number works) before the data leaves you. Keep the list that links codes to names inside the organisation.

candidates.cost: No link back to the person at all.
candidates.how: Remove names, codes and anything that could single someone out. Only possible when nothing needs to go back to a person.

candidates.cost: The health, SEND or other special category details stay out.
candidates.how: Strip those details before the data goes anywhere, or keep that part in an organisation system.

candidates.cost: Only structured fields go in; no open text or recordings.
candidates.how: Use a form with fixed answers instead of a comments box or recording.

candidates.cost: Someone has to check each outcome.
candidates.how: Add a step where a named role reviews each result before it counts.
Make sure staff can change any output before it is used.

candidates.cost: Switch tool to the approved one.
candidates.how: Use the sanctioned route for this tier instead.

levers.note: Every lever on the canvas. One plain sentence and one example each. 'face' levers show on the node; the rest open in the drawer. A lever with no rule using it should not be here.

people.label: ages
people.sentence: Are any of the people this is about under 18, and how young? Every under-18 counts as a child in law; under 13 they can't consent to an online service themselves.
people.example: A Level 3 class with 16 and 19 year olds is '16 to 18'; a Year 6 class is 'under 13'.

people.label: vulnerable
people.sentence: Are they in a position where they can't easily say no or understand what's happening?

data.label: names on it
data.sentence: Can you tell who someone is from this?
data.example: Names means their name is on it; coded means a code you can look up; anonymous means nobody can look up who it is; totals means numbers only.

data.label: says how they're doing
data.sentence: Does it say anything about a named person's performance, progress, behaviour or needs?

data.label: health, SEND or similar
data.sentence: Does it reveal health, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, union membership, biometrics, or criminal matters?
data.example: SEND notes, a sick note, a dietary requirement that reveals religion.

data.label: free text or audio
data.sentence: Does it include open text or recordings where anything could be written or said?

data.label: held for another reason
data.sentence: Did you already have this data for a different reason?
data.example: Attendance data now used to predict dropout.

data.label: newly collected
data.sentence: Are you collecting something you didn't collect before?
data.example: A new form, a new login.

data.label: they use it themselves
data.sentence: Will the people it's about use the tool themselves?
data.example: A revision app students log into.

purpose.label: scores people
purpose.sentence: Does it produce a mark, grade, score, rank or prediction about a person?
purpose.example: A suggested grade, a risk score, a 'likely to pass' flag.

purpose.label: decides without a human
purpose.sentence: Could the outcome happen with nobody checking it?
purpose.example: An automatic fail, an automatic referral.

purpose.label: staff can override
purpose.sentence: Can a person change every output before it counts?
purpose.example: A teacher can alter any suggested mark.

purpose.label: people have been told
purpose.sentence: Have the people been told about this use, somewhere they'd see it?
purpose.example: A line in the student privacy notice.

purpose.label: ongoing
purpose.sentence: Does it keep running rather than happen once?

purpose.label: whole cohort
purpose.sentence: Does it cover everyone in a large group?
purpose.example: All students in a college vs one class.

purpose.label: tracks behaviour
purpose.sentence: Does it log what individuals do, where they are, or what they click?
purpose.example: Login times per student, location, browsing.

purpose.label: can block access
purpose.sentence: Could it stop someone getting a service or exercising a right?

system.label: is AI
system.sentence: Does it use AI, machine learning or generative models anywhere?
system.example: Copilot, AI Builder, a model behind an app.

system.label: it hands back
system.example: A draft email; a suggested mark; a score; a pass or fail.

system.label: a person checks it
system.sentence: Does someone check the output before it's used?
system.example: A teacher reads the feedback before it goes out.

system.label: staff can override
system.sentence: Can a person change any output?
system.example: A teacher edits the suggested feedback before sending.

system.label: plan
system.sentence: Which plan is this tool on? The same product is a different thing on each: free and personal plans usually train on what you type and come with no contract.
system.example: Free ChatGPT trains on your chats; ChatGPT Business doesn't, and comes with a data protection agreement.

company.label: role
company.sentence: Who decides what happens to the data?
company.example: Microsoft running Copilot on your instructions is a processor; a partner school you share with is joint.

company.label: decides the purpose
company.sentence: Does this company choose why the data is used?
company.example: A partner that runs its own research on the data.

company.label: decides the means
company.sentence: Does this company choose how it's processed?
company.example: A supplier that picks which data to collect and how.

company.label: uses it for its own purposes
company.sentence: Does it use your data for product improvement, analytics or marketing?

company.label: trains on your data
company.sentence: Could your data be used to train their models?
company.example: Consumer chatbots often train on chats unless you opt out.

company.label: keeps a copy
company.sentence: Do they retain prompts, uploads, outputs or logs?

role_hints.note: When these levers disagree with the chosen role, the company card says so. ICO test: who decides purpose and means.

rules.say: A processor that decides why the data is used, or uses it for itself, is acting as a controller for that part.
This company doesn't decide purpose or means, so it is probably a processor.
